paragraphs.text: An [oolong](oolong:definition) from Taiwan, dated 1980 and kept as loose leaf for forty-six years. The island has its own tradition of keeping oolong, called [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. Leaf chosen for keeping is stored cool, dry, dark and sealed, and the keeper roasts it again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, and this tea has passed both.

The record names only [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label), not a mountain or township, so it tells you where the leaf grew and nothing about height, cultivar or style. [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) began with settlers from Fujian, who brought the plants and the craft, and in the nineteenth century the island sold its oolong abroad as [Formosa Oolong](taiwan-oolong:history).

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
